source.title: SAE Interventions are Unreliable: Post-Intervention Recovery of Suppressed Behavior
source.authors: Mingyu Cui; Li Shen; Xing-Yi Yang

page_placements.theme: Error-related function can interact with or bypass SAE features

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether the SAE reconstruction residual carries behavior using component replay under an active feature clamp, rather than the original study’s measurements of error predictability and scaling.
record.gate_note: Appendix J, Table 10 reports component-replay and knockout results that directly bear on whether the SAE residual carries behavior. Other recovery outcomes, including TPP, WMDP-Bio, IOI, and the main refusal-recovery results, are not separately recorded here because they do not isolate the reconstruction-error component.
record.test_reason: The study does not measure what any version names. Its 'SAE residual' is the SAE-unexplained part of an optimized adversarial perturbation δx. That perturbation is built to restore a clamped behaviour, and the clamp itself keeps the natural SAE error by design (Sec. 3). No row measures behaviour lost when the model's own SAE error is dropped from a feature-based circuit or steering analysis (V5). None measures linear predictability, scaling, loss under splicing, or training effects (V1–V4, V6). The behaviour is induced on purpose by gradient optimization under projection constraints, and those constraints push δx away from the clamped feature directions, so the result is partly shaped by construction. It is a related construct: an adversarial recovery path lies largely outside the SAE's span. The authors discuss its implications for reading reconstruction error ('not inert error'), but this is not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. One clarification is needed: the 'SAE reconstruction residual' that carries recovery is the SAE-unexplained component of the optimized recovery perturbation δx, shown in a single Gemma-2B refusal setting with 24 prompts. The authors conclude that SAE feature clamps are useful causal handles but not complete bottlenecks. They also say the residual channel is not inert error and can carry behaviourally sufficient information.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses constrained post-intervention residual optimization and component replay under an active SAE clamp. It does not measure linear predictability or error scaling across SAE sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that recovery rates and base-like recovery change with the number of clamped refusal features; in the broader feature-set regime, base-like recovery falls as the clamp becomes more disruptive.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma-2B under an active refusal clamp, replaying only the SAE-unexplained part of an optimized recovery perturbation restores non-refusal on 23/24 prompts (14/24 base-like). Replaying non-clamped SAE-feature changes restores 2/24, and clamped-feature changes restore 0/24.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimized perturbations that recover clamp-suppressed behaviour route mainly through directions outside the SAE's reconstruction span, not through alternative SAE latents.

record.problems: The main refusal attribution uses only 24 strict-valid AdvBench prompts. The authors state that manual labels are pending and that the automatic refusal-opening metrics do not establish response quality. The diagnostic is white-box and uses optimized per-input perturbations; generalization across models, prompts, clamps, and SAE releases remains untested.
record.rows_left_out: No Table 10 component replay or knockout outcomes were left out. Other experiments and refusal recovery totals were not extracted as rows because they do not isolate the SAE reconstruction residual component.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from the input is not measured.
Error-norm prediction across SAE sizes and shared failure contexts are not measured.
No comparison of spliced-in loss against random errors of the same size.
No split into linear and nonlinear error, and no further dictionary learning.
No measure of how much behaviour a feature-based circuit or steering analysis loses when the model's natural SAE error is omitted. Clamps keep the error term throughout.
No SAE architectures or training objectives are compared; all SAEs are frozen.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V5 and labelled it supports/limits_scope. That linkage is rejected: the study's residual differs from the natural SAE error in the original source, and the intervention keeps the error term. The projection constraints (encoder orthogonality, Jacobian) bias δx away from the clamped feature directions, which may partly explain why recovery sits outside the SAE span. The other experiments (TPP, WMDP-Bio, IOI, HarmBench, the K sweep) concern recoverability of clamp-suppressed behaviour and bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure how much SAE error is linearly predictable from input activations.
The study does not test per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, shared failure contexts across sizes, or whether error norms vanish with scale.
The study does not compare model loss after SAE reconstruction replacement with loss after random errors of the same size.
The study does not separate linearly predictable and nonlinear error, or test whether either part reflects unlearned features or resists further dictionary learning.

It tests whether the SAE reconstruction residual can carry refusal-recovery behavior in one model and setting, not whether circuits or steering analyses generally lose behavior when the error term is omitted.
The study does not compare SAE training objectives or architectures, or test whether improved or end-to-end training shrinks the reconstruction residual.

relation.reason: The discussion argues that SAE-unexplained residual directions can carry behavior, but the experiments concern optimized perturbations rather than behavior lost when natural SAE reconstruction error is omitted.

tranche.reason: The experiments optimize recovery perturbations under selected-feature clamps and attribute those perturbations. They do not measure any claim version's quantity; the natural activation reconstruction error is preserved throughout.

source_check.notes: Appendix J defines the residual component as optimized δx minus its decoded SAE-feature change, rather than natural activation reconstruction error. Non-refusal is a weak opening-based readout; residual-only base-like recovery is 14/24, versus 15/24 for full replay.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2B, benchmark_our/global refusal clamp, AdvBench strict-valid prompts
reader_labels.reason: SAE-residual-only replay achieves 23/24 non-refusal recoveries and 14/24 base-like recoveries, close to full-δx replay at 23/24 and 15/24; the feature-only replays are much weaker (J5–J12).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The evidence comes from 24 strict-valid prompts, and base-like recovery from the residual replay is 14/24 rather than complete; the study does not test circuit or steering analyses broadly (J5–J6).
